To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the perception of the theoretical intractability of social psychology is due to a combination of the failure to distinguish between the validity of a social theory and its success in applied settings and to the failure to appreciate the extent to which the validity of social theories can be enhanced through the incorporation of enlightenment effects.

(a) the theoretical intractability of social psychology may be a product of the field's failure to develop formal theories and (b) the failure to develop formal social theories may in turn be due to a lack of awareness on the part of social psychologists of the need for such theories and the need for distinguishing between the validity and the applied success of a social theory.

(1) social psychologists have a tendency to overestimate their ability to explain social behavior, and (2) this tendency is related to their tendency to use the word 'theory' in an imprecise way, and to their tendency to conflate the success of their theories in highly complex applied settings with the validity of those theories as established in tightly controlled situations. In summary, our research is concerned with
the question, What is it that we are trying to explain when we try to explain human behavior?
the development of a formal, empirically testable theory of the effects of social influence processes in small group settings.
the question of whether and how social psychological theories can achieve transhistorical validity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

social theories are more difficult to test than physical theories, that this is a result of the greater complexity of the phenomena they address, and that the complexity of social phenomena is not an insuperable barrier.

social psychologists have not yet achieved transhistorical validity in their theorizing because they have not yet achieved the level of theoretical rigor and empirical sophistication necessary for such validity.
social psychologists have not made the transition to a mature science because we have not yet learned to distinguish between the validity of a theory and its success in applied settings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the field of social psychology needs a new theoretical paradigm that can be used to generate new theories that are more likely to be transhistorical in nature, that can be used in a wide variety of applied settings, and that can be used as a basis for generating more tightly controlled research designs.
social psychology has made considerable progress in developing a body of theory that is applicable to the solution of important practical problems.
social psychologists have failed to develop a theoretical tradition that is both empirically successful and conceptually rigorous.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social psychologists can and should be able to develop theories that are both highly successful in applied settings and valid in tightly controlled situations.

the failure to model such lessons has led social psychologists to underestimate the extent to which the theoretical intractabilities they perceive in social psychology are due to the failure of the field's theories to satisfy the criteria of a scientific theory.
the theoretical intractability of social psychology is not a consequence of the nature of social phenomena.
